title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Traefik ReplacePathRegex auth bypass: glued dot-dot traversal in request path AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the CVE-2026-65600 exploit signature — a path segment glued directly to a traversal sequence (e.g. /api../admin) or its percent-encoded form (/api%2e%2e/admin) that Traefik's sanitizePath accepts as a valid segment. This is the article-specific 'implicit traversal' that only fires because there is no separator before the capture group in patterns like regex '^/api(.*)'. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact exploit primitive: an alphanumeric segment immediately followed by '..' with no separator (api../admin) plus the PoC's URL-encoded variant %2e%2e. Normal clients almost never send a glued dot-dot, and standard /../ is excluded by requiring an alnum char before the dots, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-65600/
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, Nessus) probing for path traversal against the reverse proxy
  • Legitimate WAF/pentest validation traffic replaying the PoC path
  • Applications that legitimately embed literal '..' in a non-path query parameter that gets logged in the URL field
  • Broken clients double-encoding paths that happen to contain %2e%2e
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-scanner-ips>") | where not (HttpHostName has_any ("vulnscan","security-testing"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP; confirm the RawPath glues a real config prefix to '..' and note the returned status — a 2xx to a normally-protected route is a confirmed bypass. 2) Contain: place the vulnerable router/middleware behind a temporary deny rule for paths matching the traversal regex, or block the source IP at the edge; schedule upgrade to Traefik 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7. 3) Hunt: enumerate all ReplacePathRegex middlewares with unbounded capture groups (^/x(.*)), then review backend logs for prior 2xx on protected routes reached via traversal.
let lookback = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| extend RawPath = tostring(coalesce(UrlOriginal, Url))
| where RawPath matches regex @"(?i)[a-z0-9]\.\.(/|%2f|$)" or RawPath contains "%2e%2e" or RawPath contains "%2E%2E"   // glued dot-dot or encoded traversal — CVE-2026-65600 signature
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, RawPath, HttpStatusCode, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Traefik path-traversal bypass CONFIRMED: traversal request returns 2xx on protected route AIActions on Objectives High
Impact-confirmation for CVE-2026-65600. Surfaces requests that carry the glued/encoded traversal signature AND received a 2xx response — meaning the backend normalized /../admin to /admin and served protected content without the auth middleware ever running. This separates blocked probes from a successful authentication bypass. Rationale: Combines the traversal path signature with an HTTP 2xx status — the article states the backend normalizes /../admin to /admin and returns ADMIN_SECRET_DATA, so a success response on a traversal path is a high-fidelity bypass confirmation rather than a mere probe. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanners that trigger a generic 200 error/landing page rather than real protected content
  • Backends that echo the raw path in a 200 without actually serving the protected resource
  • Load-balancer health probes hitting a permissive catch-all route
  • URLs where '..' appears in a query string the app ignores but still returns 200
Suppression filter
| where not (RawPath has_any ("/health","/healthz","/favicon.ico"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the 2xx body/route is genuinely a protected resource (admin/config/internal API) and not a generic page; capture the exact RawPath and normalized target. 2) Contain: treat as active compromise — rotate any credentials/secrets exposed on the reached route, block the source IP, and hot-patch the middleware to reject non-normalizing paths pending upgrade. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP and session across all backends for further 2xx traversal hits, and review protected-route access logs for the full window since the vulnerable config was deployed.

Traefik dynamic config write introducing unbounded ReplacePathRegex capture group AIWeaponization Medium
Detects creation/modification of Traefik configuration files (traefik.yml/.toml, dynamic.yml, /etc/traefik/) — the deployment vector for the vulnerable ReplacePathRegex pattern '^/api(.*)' with replacement '/$1'. Endpoint telemetry flags the file touch; pair with a content audit of the written file for the separator-less capture group. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete config filenames and the /etc/traefik/ mount path from the PoC docker-compose. This is coarse (endpoint telemetry cannot read the regex content), so it is a hunting-tier trigger to drive a content audit for the vulnerable '^/api(.*)' + '/$1' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv
ATT&CKT1190 T1526
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine GitOps/CI deployment of Traefik config via Ansible/Helm/kustomize
  • Admin manually tuning routers/middlewares
  • Container image rebuilds that rewrite the mounted config
  • Config-reload tooling touching the file on every restart
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("helm.exe","ansible","kustomize","dockerd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and search for ReplacePathRegex middlewares whose regex captures without a mandatory separator (e.g. ^/prefix(.*)) and whose replacement re-emits the capture (/$1). 2) Contain: correct the pattern to include the slash (^/prefix/(.*)) or upgrade Traefik to a patched release that rejects non-normalizing paths. 3) Hunt: inventory all clusters/hosts running the same config template and check web logs for prior traversal exploitation against those routers.

Token Jacking: Cybercriminals Could Be Stealing Your AI Resources

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)

Discover how attackers hijack AI tokens to fuel gray market transfer stations by stealing developer API keys. The post Token Jacking: Cybercriminals Could Be Stealing Your AI Resources appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AI resource key creation paired with logging/alert teardown in cloud control plane
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound traffic to known AI token-jacking transfer-station infrastructure (Unit42 IPs) · [LLM] Transfer-station client fingerprint: Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe) user-agent in web egress · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Outbound traffic to known AI token-jacking transfer-station infrastructure (Unit42 IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate host or cloud egress to the four IP addresses Unit 42 tied to malicious AI API calls from gray-market 'transfer stations' (new-api/one-api proxies) abusing stolen tokens. A connection from inside the environment to any of these IPs indicates either the transfer-station infrastructure being reached or a compromised host relaying stolen-token traffic. Rationale: Uses the four exact IPs from Unit 42's IOC table ('Malicious API calls'). IP-literal egress match is high-fidelity and article-specific; corroboration of the campaign economy (LLMjacking/transfer stations) via KPMG and Zscaler, though the IPs themselves are single-sourced to Unit 42. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-hosted app on 3.235.0.0/16 (AWS us-east-1) shares an IP range with legitimate SaaS — verify the exact /32
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox VMs deliberately connecting to flagged IPs
  • A security researcher in the org validating the IOCs
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign tenant (IOC decay — confirm timestamp vs. article publish date)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the internal src host/user and the process that made the connection; confirm the dst is the exact /32 and note bytes transferred (large volume = active token relay). 2) CONTAIN: Block the four IPs at egress/firewall, isolate the source host, and immediately rotate/revoke any AI provider API keys reachable from that host. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for infostealer/npm-worm artifacts (Shai-Hulud/Miasma), search for the Go-http-client UA in proxy logs, and audit AI-provider consoles for unauthorized key creation and disabled billing alerts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("3.235.109.125","116.105.166.148","172.96.142.186","38.46.219.166")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("3.235.109.125","116.105.166.148","172.96.142.186","38.46.219.166")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count() by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, RequestClientApplication
| order by LastSeen desc

Transfer-station client fingerprint: Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe) user-agent in web egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the exact HTTP User-Agent string Unit 42 tied to malicious AI API calls made by transfer-station proxies (new-api/one-api). Its appearance in outbound web/proxy telemetry — especially toward AI provider API endpoints — flags stolen-token abuse or a compromised host acting as an API relay. Rationale: Uses the verbatim User-Agent from Unit 42's IOC table. The 'gzip(gfe)' suffix (Google Frontend) on a Go default client is an unusual fingerprint for corporate egress; medium confidence because bare Go clients are legit, so pair with AI-API destination domains during triage. Defender/Falcon left empty — their network telemetry does not carry the HTTP User-Agent header. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal Go microservices/CI jobs using the default net/http client that traverse a GFE-fronted API
  • Go-based SDKs calling Google/GCP services (the gzip(gfe) marker comes from Google Frontend)
  • Monitoring/uptime agents written in Go
  • Homegrown API integrations that never set a custom UA
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname has_any ("openai","anthropic","googleapis","generativelanguage","api.x.ai","deepseek")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Enumerate the destination domains for this UA — legitimate internal Go services should hit known APIs; hits to LLM provider endpoints (OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini) with this UA are the true positive. 2) CONTAIN: If the destination is an AI API and the source is not a sanctioned service, revoke the API keys used from that host and block the flow. 3) HUNT: Correlate the source with UC1 IP hits and with any recent npm install activity (Shai-Hulud/Miasma) or infostealer detections on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has "Go-http-client/2.0,gzip(gfe)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), Domains=make_set(DstHostname, 20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by Requests desc

AI resource key creation paired with logging/alert teardown in cloud control plane AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the developer-account abuse Unit 42 lists: attackers who steal privileged AI/cloud credentials then create new API keys and disable usage alerts/logging so token theft stays invisible until the bill arrives. Detects the same principal regenerating/creating keys on an AI (Cognitive Services / Bedrock) resource while deleting diagnostic or model-invocation logging in a short window. Rationale: Directly operationalizes the article's four enumerated developer-account abuses ('Creating new API keys', 'Provisioning models', 'Disabling critical usage alerts and logging') as concrete Azure Cognitive Services and AWS Bedrock control-plane operations. The key-creation + logging-delete combo within a window is the article-specific behavioral signal, not a generic admin action. Defender/Falcon/Sigma left empty — this is cloud audit telemetry not in Defender XDR endpoint tables, and it's a multi-op correlation unsuited to single-event Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ai-token-jacking/ • https://kpmg.com/us/en/articles/2026/ai-emerging-threat.html
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1562.008 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform team rotating Cognitive Services keys during scheduled secret rotation
  • IaC/Terraform runs that recreate diagnostic settings (delete then re-add) in the same window
  • Legitimate model deployment change alongside a logging config refresh
  • AWS admin reconfiguring Bedrock model-invocation logging destination (delete + re-put)
  • Break-glass/service-principal automation that legitimately manages keys and logs together
Suppression filter
| where Caller !endswith "terraform" and Caller !has "iac-" and CallerIpAddress != ""
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Caller/CallerIpAddress is expected — check whether the same principal both created/rotated a key AND deleted logging (benign rotation re-adds logging; malicious tears it down). Review the source IP against UC1 IOCs and geolocation. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the newly created/regenerated key, re-enable diagnostic/model-invocation logging, and force credential reset on the developer/service account. 3) HUNT: Query AI provider usage/billing for a token-consumption spike, and trace how the account credential was obtained (infostealer, phishing, or npm worm) on the developer's endpoint.
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActivityStatusValue == "Success"
| where OperationNameValue in~ (
    "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/regenerateKey/action",
    "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/listKeys/action",
    "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write",
    "Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete")
| summarize Ops=make_set(OperationNameValue), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by Caller, CallerIpAddress, ResourceGroup, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Ops has "Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete" and (Ops has "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/regenerateKey/action" or Ops has "Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write")
| order by LastSeen desc

| filter eventSource in ["bedrock.amazonaws.com","iam.amazonaws.com"]

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

status: experimental
description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Nuxt dev server bound to non-loopback interface (nuxi/nuxt dev --host) · [LLM] Inbound non-loopback connection to Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe HMR port)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe) spawns shell or LOLBin child — DevTools RPC RCE

Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe) spawns shell or LOLBin child — DevTools RPC RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the payload-execution step of CVE-2026-71319, where the unauthenticated openInEditor()/updateOptions() RPC chain makes the launch-editor package spawn an attacker-controlled command as a child of the node.exe dev server. Scopes to node.exe whose command line indicates a Nuxt/Vite dev process spawning an interpreter or LOLBin — a combination that should never occur during normal 'nuxi dev'. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete chain (openInEditor -> launch-editor spawns child of the node.exe dev server) plus the specific process ancestry (node.exe parent whose cmdline contains nuxt/nuxi/vite/devtools -> interpreter/LOLBin child). Cross-checked GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv and the Nuxt v4.5 security blog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://nuxt.com/blog/v4-5-security • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nuxt/devtools/CVE-2026-71319/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately configured 'openInEditor' to a shell wrapper that launches their editor (e.g. a cmd/powershell shim launching VS Code)
  • Nuxt/Vite build scripts invoking curl.exe to fetch assets during dev
  • A dev-tooling task runner spawning powershell for a lifecycle hook (postinstall-style scripts run via node)
  • node-based test runners shelling out to cmd.exe for OS-level test fixtures
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "code.exe" and ProcessCommandLine !has "code-insiders" and ProcessCommandLine !has "sublime_text" and ProcessCommandLine !has "webstorm" and ProcessCommandLine !has "idea64.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine. A benign hit shows an editor path (code.exe, sublime); a malicious hit shows arbitrary commands (whoami, curl to external IP, base64, reverse-shell one-liners). Confirm the node.exe process is a nuxi/vite dev server. 2) Contain: kill the node dev-server process tree, isolate the developer workstation, and force-update @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1 (lockfile refresh). 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound non-loopback connections to the node.exe listening port just before the spawn, and review the child process's own children/network egress for follow-on payloads or credential access.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite",".nuxt","devtools")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite",".nuxt","devtools")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","curl.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nuxt/Vite Dev Server node.exe Spawns Shell or LOLBin (CVE-2026-71319)
id: 6f2b1c9a-8d34-4e21-9a0f-0b7c2e5d9a11
description: Detects node.exe running a Nuxt/Vite dev server spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin, matching the launch-editor RCE chain in CVE-2026-71319.
references:
  - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv
  - https://nuxt.com/blog/v4-5-security
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/06
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\node.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'nuxt'
      - 'nuxi'
      - 'vite'
      - 'devtools'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE) (@ParentCommandLine:*nuxt* OR @ParentCommandLine:*nuxi* OR @ParentCommandLine:*vite* OR @ParentCommandLine:*devtools*) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/node\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bash|curl)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","calc.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","calc.exe","curl.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Nuxt dev server bound to non-loopback interface (nuxi/nuxt dev --host) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the risky exposure configuration the CVE-2026-71319 advisory explicitly warns against: running the dev server with '--host', which binds the Vite HMR / DevTools RPC socket to a non-loopback interface and makes the unauthenticated RPC channel reachable by any LAN peer. This is a posture/initial-access hunt for exposed dev servers before exploitation. Rationale: Directly encodes the advisory's named risky invocation 'nuxi dev --host' as the exposure signal — it is the one config that turns a same-host-only bug into a LAN-reachable RCE. High-signal because '--host' on a dev command is deliberate and uncommon. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://nuxt.com/blog/v4-5-security
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer intentionally using --host to test on a mobile device over the same Wi-Fi
  • CI/preview pipelines that bind dev servers with --host inside an isolated container network
  • Team using --host on a trusted, firewalled dev VLAN by policy
  • Docker-based dev where --host is required for port forwarding to reach the container
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is on an untrusted/shared network and whether @nuxt/devtools is < 3.3.1 on that project. Note the listening port from the command line. 2) Contain: advise the developer to drop --host (or restrict to loopback), or patch @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1 / set devtools:{enabled:false}. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (node.exe spawning interpreters) and to inbound connections on the dev-server port from non-loopback sources on this host during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxi","nuxt")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dev"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--host"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxi","nuxt")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dev"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--host"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nuxt Dev Server Bound to Non-Loopback Interface (--host) CVE-2026-71319 Exposure
id: b3a71e28-4c19-4d77-8e5a-2f9c6d1b7e42
description: Detects nuxi/nuxt dev started with --host, which exposes the unauthenticated Vite HMR DevTools RPC channel (CVE-2026-71319) to LAN peers.
references:
  - https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/06
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1133
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'dev'
      - '--host'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'nuxi'
      - 'nuxt'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:*nuxi* OR @CommandLine:*nuxt*) @CommandLine:*dev* @CommandLine:*--host*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(nuxi|nuxt)/i
| CommandLine=/\bdev\b/i
| CommandLine=/--host/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*dev*" AND Processes.process="*--host*" AND (Processes.process="*nuxi*" OR Processes.process="*nuxt*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*dev*" AND Processes.process="*--host*" AND (Processes.process="*nuxi*" OR Processes.process="*nuxt*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound non-loopback connection to Nuxt/Vite dev server (node.exe HMR port) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a remote peer connecting to the Vite HMR / DevTools RPC listener hosted by node.exe from a non-loopback address — the network precondition for CVE-2026-71319 exploitation over the LAN. Because the vulnerable RPC channel is normally only reached via localhost, any inbound accept from a non-loopback source to a nuxt/vite node process is anomalous and worth pairing with UC1. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's stated LAN reach ('any peer on the LAN when the dev server is bound with nuxi dev --host'). Scopes inbound accepts to node.exe dev processes and excludes loopback, isolating the exact network shape an off-host attacker must produce. Sentinel left blank: no available tenant table reliably attributes inbound socket accepts to the node.exe process. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-279x-mwfv-vcqv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nuxt/devtools/CVE-2026-71319/
ATT&CKT1190 T1021
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing the site from a phone/tablet on the same LAN hitting the dev server
  • Another workstation on the dev subnet legitimately previewing a colleague's dev build
  • Container/host networking where the bridge presents a non-loopback source IP for local traffic
  • Local network scanners / asset-inventory tools probing the open dev port
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteIP — is it a known developer device or an unexpected/unknown LAN host? Check what LocalPort node.exe was listening on and whether --host was used (UC2). 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, isolate the workstation, kill the node dev server, and patch @nuxt/devtools to >=3.3.1. 3) Hunt: correlate the inbound connection timestamp with UC1 (node.exe spawning an interpreter/LOLBin) on the same host within a short window — a spawn shortly after the inbound accept is strong evidence of successful RPC exploitation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite","devtools")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback")
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("nuxt","nuxi","vite","devtools")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback")
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i ConnectionDirection=1
| NOT (RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./ OR LocalAddressIP4=/^127\./)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" AND All_Traffic.direction="inbound" AND NOT (All_Traffic.src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1"))) by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" AND All_Traffic.direction="inbound" AND NOT (All_Traffic.src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1"))) by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.

From open lures to cloaked gates: How a macOS ClickFix campaign learned to hide

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-05 12 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A macOS ClickFix campaign shifted tactics from openly serving infostealer lures to hiding them behind a browser-fingerprinting gate. The change makes malicious infrastructure harder to detect while giving defenders new hunting opportunities. The post From open lures to cloaked gates: How a macOS ClickFix campaign learned to hide appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1027 T1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

A credential-stealing worm hidden in more than 400 compromised npm packages automatically spread across software ecosystems by republishing malicious updates. npm preinstall lifecycle hook launching 'node setup.mjs' (ChainDrop/Shai-Hulud loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ChainDrop worm's execution primitive: a compromised npm package whose preinstall hook launches the embedded setup.mjs loader via node. This is the exact string ('node setup.mjs') published by Microsoft Threat Intelligence and is the earliest on-host signal of an affected package install. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim 'node setup.mjs' invocation and the npm preinstall parent context published by Microsoft; corroborated by StepSecurity and Zscaler analyses of the same setup.mjs loader. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal package whose author happens to ship a benign setup.mjs run at preinstall
  • Monorepo bootstrap scripts that call a locally-named setup.mjs
  • Developer running a hand-written build helper named setup.mjs from a project root
  • CI base-image provisioning that legitimately shells node against a setup.mjs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("run build","run bootstrap") and FolderPath has_any (@"\corp-internal\", @"\company-monorepo\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the alerting host/runner, pull the full parent chain and the package/tarball being installed (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and hash setup.mjs against the article IOCs (54dc7ea5..., fd3ca400...). Confirm whether it was an npm/yarn/pnpm install. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the workstation/build runner and immediately revoke+rotate every credential reachable from that identity (npm publish token, GitHub PAT/OIDC, AWS keys, Vault, kube) from a known-clean host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to bun execution (UC2), outbound to npm-cache.com (UC4), IMDS reads (UC6), and any npm publish originating from this host (UC7).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","bun","bun.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci","npm-cli.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm","bun") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm ci")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
