setup.mjs spawning Bun runtime to execute obfuscated payload from node_modules/bun-dl AIInstallation High
Hunts stage-2 of ChainDrop: the setup.mjs loader launching the Bun runtime to run the heavily-obfuscated ~728KB Math_*.js credential-stealer, executing from a node_modules path or a 'bun-dl-' download directory. Bun as a child of a node/setup.mjs install context is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the article's Block-2 pivot (bun child of node setup.mjs, bun-dl- folder, node_modules) plus the corroborated Math_*.js payload name; Bun in an npm-install process tree is a rare, high-fidelity artifact of this specific worm. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared
ATT&CKT1027 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teams that legitimately use Bun as their JS runtime/bundler in local dev
  • CI pipelines that install Bun via a bun-dl style downloader for legitimate builds
  • A developer manually testing a Bun script located under node_modules
  • Bun-based test runners invoked by a project's own tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","bun.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun test","bun run dev") and not (ProcessCommandLine has "Math_"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun binary path and hash; check whether the org uses Bun at all and whether the parent was setup.mjs. Grab the payload path (Math_*.js) and hash it. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner; treat all identity material as exposed and rotate from clean infra. 3) HUNT: Look for outbound to oven-sh/bun releases (bun download), C2 to npm-cache.com/pypi-get.com (UC4), and IMDS/credential enumeration (UC6) on the same host within minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","Math_",".js")
   or FolderPath contains "bun-dl-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules","bun-dl-","Math_")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop known-bad file drop: setup.mjs / Math_*.js hashes on disk AIInstallation Medium
Signature-grade detection on the three Microsoft-published SHA256 hashes for the ChainDrop setup.mjs loaders and the Math_*.js payload landing on a workstation or build runner. Deterministic confirmation an affected tarball was unpacked/executed. Rationale: Pure IOC match on the three Microsoft-published ChainDrop SHA256 values (setup.mjs loader variants + Math_*.js); zero interpretation risk and confirmed in the article's IOC table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher deliberately storing the sample for analysis on a sandbox host
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-hashing on a scanning host
  • Backup/forensic image mount replaying the file into DeviceFileEvents
  • Threat-intel sharing folder holding the IOC sample
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","ir-analysis") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a live dev/CI system rather than a sandbox/IR analysis box; identify InitiatingProcess that wrote the file. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate; rotate all credentials accessible to the affected identity from clean infrastructure and pull the associated npm package/version for removal from internal mirrors. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all hosts that installed the same package version; check for downstream republish (UC7) and exfil (UC4).

ChainDrop C2 exfiltration from node/bun to npm-cache.com / pypi-get.com / js-mirror.com AICommand & Control High
Detects the encrypted exfiltration channel: node or bun contacting the ChainDrop attacker-controlled HTTPS endpoints (npm-cache.com, pypi-get.com, js-mirror.com) to POST AES-256-GCM/RSA-OAEP encrypted credential bundles. Process-scoped to the worm runtimes to keep it high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the three exfil C2 domains from the article's pre-extracted IOCs and IOC table, scoped to the node/bun runtimes that actually perform exfiltration; npm-cache.com is independently confirmed as the HTTPS fallback endpoint by hackread/Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://hackread.com/shai-hulud-npm-worm-poisoning-1280-packages/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal package registry mirror coincidentally named similarly (verify exact FQDN)
  • Security tooling detonating the sample and generating the C2 lookups from a sandbox
  • Threat-intel enrichment services resolving the IOC domains for reputation checks
  • DNS sinkhole/passive-DNS collectors resolving the domain for logging
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","threatintel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the resolving/connecting process is node/bun and the source is a real dev/CI host; capture bytes-out and destination. 2) CONTAIN: Block the three domains at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and rotate every credential reachable from that identity (npm, GitHub, AWS, Vault, kube) from clean infra — assume exfiltration succeeded. 3) HUNT: Check for GitHub fallback exfil (new public repo described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again', results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json commits), IMDS reads (UC6), and republish activity (UC7).

ChainDrop IMDS credential theft: node/bun reading cloud instance metadata (169.254.169.254 / 169.254.170.2) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ChainDrop credential-enumeration behaviour where the Bun/node payload calls cloud instance-metadata endpoints to steal AWS/ECS role credentials on build runners. A JS runtime hitting link-local IMDS is highly abnormal outside SDK-driven app code and is a strong signal on a compromised runner. Rationale: The article describes AWS/Kubernetes/Vault credential enumeration via API calls; second sources (Wiz/hackread) explicitly list IMDS reads from 169.254.169.254 and 169.254.170.2 by build agents as a ChainDrop IOC. Scoping to node/bun cuts SDK/app-driven metadata noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://hackread.com/shai-hulud-npm-worm-poisoning-1280-packages/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node.js app on an EC2/ECS host using the AWS SDK, which reads IMDS for role credentials
  • CI runner tooling written in Bun that legitimately queries ECS task metadata (169.254.170.2)
  • Health/monitoring agents embedded in a node service polling instance metadata
  • aws-sdk-js credential provider chain doing routine IMDSv2 token fetches
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","preinstall") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node.exe","bun.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine if the node/bun process is a legitimate long-running app (SDK) or an install-time process spawned from setup.mjs/npm. Correlate timing with a package install and UC1/UC2 hits. 2) CONTAIN: If tied to install, isolate the runner and immediately rotate the instance/role credentials and any Vault/kube secrets reachable; disable the affected role's active sessions. 3) HUNT: Trace what the stolen role could reach (S3, secrets manager, CloudTrail AssumeRole), and check for exfil (UC4) and republish (UC7).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where SrcUsername != "" or isnotempty(SrcHostname)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop persistence: node/bun injecting .claude and .vscode config files into repositories AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ChainDrop persistence and developer-to-developer spread mechanism where the payload writes malicious Claude (.claude/) and Visual Studio Code (.vscode/) configuration files into local repositories. Scoped to writes performed by the node/bun worm runtimes to separate from normal IDE activity. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated persistence/spread routine (inject .claude and .vscode config files via the loader hash fd3ca400...), constrained to node/bun writers driven by setup.mjs to reduce normal IDE churn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://www.upwind.io/feed/shai-hulud-2-npm-supply-chain-worm-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VS Code or an extension legitimately writing .vscode/settings.json during project setup
  • A dev tool scaffolding a .claude/ config as part of normal onboarding
  • postinstall scripts of legitimate packages that write editor config
  • A formatter/linter run via node updating .vscode config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code.exe","Code.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("eslint","prettier","scaffold"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the written .claude/.vscode files for injected commands/hooks and confirm the writer was a setup.mjs/npm-install context, not the user's IDE. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, remove the injected config across all repo branches, and rotate GitHub credentials/tokens used by the identity. 3) HUNT: Check git history for pushed .claude/.vscode changes from this identity, and pivot to any repos the token could write to.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\", "/.claude/", @"\.vscode\", "/.vscode/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node.exe","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.claude/", "\\.claude\\", "/.vscode/", "\\.vscode\\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChainDrop .claude and .vscode config injection by node or bun

ChainDrop worm propagation: npm publish spawned from a package-install context AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the self-propagation routine where the ChainDrop payload uses a stolen npm token to republish tarballs: an 'npm publish' (or programmatic publish) invoked as a child of the node/bun worm runtime or from within node_modules, rather than an interactive developer release. This is the mechanism turning one compromised identity into hundreds of malicious releases. Rationale: Targets the article's core propagation routine ('After obtaining an npm publishing token... republishes the modified packages'): a publish command parented by the worm runtime / originating from node_modules rather than an interactive dev shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate CI release pipeline running 'npm publish' from a node-based release script
  • semantic-release / np / changesets tooling publishing programmatically via node
  • A developer publishing from a monorepo where the script runs under node_modules tooling
  • Internal automation republishing scoped packages to a private registry
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("semantic-release","changeset","np ") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","Math_")))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether this publish belongs to a sanctioned release pipeline; check the parent chain for setup.mjs/bun and whether it ran on a dev workstation vs. release runner. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the npm publishing token immediately and place a publish hold; isolate the host. Check npm for versions published by this identity with no matching git commit/tag. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every package the token could publish, diff recently-published versions for injected preinstall/setup.mjs, and notify the registry to yank malicious versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName in~ ("npm","npm.cmd") and ProcessCommandLine has "publish")
     or (FileName in~ ("node","node.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("npm","publish"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules","Math_")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "node_modules"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "npm"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun") or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","node_modules") or ActingProcessCommandLine has "node_modules"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChainDrop worm npm publish from install context
id: 9a4d6e33-5c71-4b28-8f09-2d7b1c6a3f07
description: Detects an npm publish invoked as a child of the node/bun worm runtime or from within node_modules, characteristic of ChainDrop self-propagation
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'npm'
      - 'publish'
  selection_ctx:
    - ParentImage|endswith:
        - '/node'
        - '\node.exe'
        - '/bun'
        - '\bun.exe'
    - ParentCommandLine|contains: 'setup.mjs'
    - CommandLine|contains: 'node_modules'
  condition: selection_cmd and selection_ctx
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*npm*publish* OR *"npm publish"*) (@ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\bun.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\BUN.EXE) OR @ParentCommandLine:*setup.mjs* OR @CommandLine:*node_modules*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("npm.*publish", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(node|bun)(\.exe)?$/i OR regex("setup\.mjs|node_modules", field=ParentCommandLine) OR regex("node_modules", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe") OR like(parent_process, "%setup.mjs%") OR like(parent_process, "%node_modules%") OR like(process, "%node_modules%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process_name IN ("npm","npm.cmd","node","node.exe"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","bun","bun.exe") OR like(parent_process, "%setup.mjs%") OR like(parent_process, "%node_modules%") OR like(process, "%node_modules%")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| sort - files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Unauthenticated Flowise OAuth2 token-refresh endpoint access from external source (CVE-2026-70478) AIExploitation High
Hunts external/public source IPs POSTing to the whitelisted, no-auth Flowise endpoint /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId and receiving HTTP 200, which returns the connected-service access_token in the body. Article-specific to the exact vulnerable route and its successful-response shape. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable route '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/' with POST + HTTP 200 (the article states a valid ID returns the new access_token in the body, while unknown IDs return 'Credential not found'). External source filter (ipv4_is_private) removes the app's own frontend, which is the legitimate caller. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: no web-access-log table exists in Defender XDR (DeviceNetworkEvents lacks URL path), FDR ships no HTTP path, and this is not AWS-native telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478 • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/flowise-unauthenticated-oauth-secrets-disclosure-via-api-v1-loginmethod-endpoint
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Azure App Service platform health-check probes hitting the app root (filter by UserAgent)
  • Legitimate Flowise UI running on a public IP not covered by RFC1918 (SaaS/cloud-hosted analyst workstation)
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites CIp to the proxy's own address, masking true client and collapsing all traffic to one IP
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling authorised to probe the app
  • Load balancer synthetic monitoring calling the API
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "AlwaysOn" and UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "Edge Health Probe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all rows for the offending CIp — confirm the source is outside your management/VPN ranges and that ScStatus==200 (token actually returned). Extract the credentialId values from CsUriStem. 2) Contain: patch Flowise to >=3.1.3 immediately (removes endpoint from WHITELIST_URLS); block the source IP at the WAF; for each exposed credentialId, revoke and rotate the linked OAuth client secret and refresh token at the provider (Google/Microsoft/GitHub). 3) Hunt: search connected-service sign-in logs (SigninLogs/CloudAppEvents) for use of the stolen access tokens from attacker infrastructure, and check for enumeration/burst patterns from the same IP (companion UCs).
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| where ScStatus == 200
| where not(ipv4_is_private(CIp))
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5) by CIp, CsHost
| order by Requests desc

Flowise OAuth2 credentialId enumeration (mixed 200/404 probing) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source probing many distinct credentialId values against the unauthenticated Flowise refresh endpoint within a short window, with a mix of HTTP 200 (valid IDs) and 404/403 (misses) — the discovery step the attacker uses to find live credential IDs before token theft. Rationale: Article's Docker validation shows unknown IDs return 'Credential not found' (a 4xx) while valid IDs succeed, so a burst of distinct credentialId path values with a 200/miss mix on this exact route is the enumeration fingerprint. 5-in-2-minutes threshold separates scanning from a user's single-credential UI refresh. Aggregation/threshold logic so no Sigma; not Defender/FDR/AWS telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-70478
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin bulk-refreshing many stored credentials from the Flowise UI in a maintenance window
  • Automated internal job that iterates credentials to keep tokens warm
  • Broken frontend retry loop hammering the endpoint with the same/few IDs (would show low distinct-ID count — tune threshold)
  • Web vulnerability scanner authorised against the app generating 404s across guessed paths
  • CDN/proxy collapsing multiple real users to one egress IP
Suppression filter
| where CIp !in (dynamic([]))  // populate with known maintenance/automation egress IPs after first tuning pass
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct credentialId values the source requested and their status codes — a wide spread of UUIDs with 404s confirms enumeration; note which returned 200. 2) Contain: block the source IP; upgrade to Flowise >=3.1.3; rotate secrets for any credentialId that returned 200 during the burst. 3) Hunt: pivot to the burst-refresh UC for the same IP to see if enumeration was followed by mass successful token pulls, and review connected-service logs for token misuse.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| summarize Total = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), NotFound = countif(ScStatus in (404, 403, 500)), Valid = countif(ScStatus == 200), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, bin(TimeGenerated, 2m)
| where DistinctCredIds >= 5 and NotFound >= 1   // 5+ distinct credential IDs probed in 2 min with >=1 miss = enumeration
| order by DistinctCredIds desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as total, dc(Web.url) as distinct_credids, count(eval(Web.status==404 OR Web.status==403 OR Web.status==500)) as misses, count(eval(Web.status==200)) as valid from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/*" by Web.src, _time span=2m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_credids >= 5 AND misses >= 1
| sort - distinct_credids
| tstats summariesonly=false count as total, dc(Web.url) as distinct_credids, count(eval(Web.status==404 OR Web.status==403 OR Web.status==500)) as misses, count(eval(Web.status==200)) as valid from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/*" by Web.src, _time span=2m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Flowise mass OAuth token harvest — burst of successful refreshes across credentials AIActions on Objectives High
Detects one source obtaining HTTP 200 refreshes for 5+ distinct credential IDs within 5 minutes on the unauthenticated Flowise endpoint — the collection-phase pattern of an attacker draining every connected-service access token after finding valid IDs. Rationale: The article states the flaw 'enables token theft for any connected service' and each 200 returns a fresh access_token; harvesting all victims means many distinct credentialId successes in a tight window. Distinct-credential threshold (>=5/5min) is what separates a mass pull from routine single-credential refreshes. Threshold correlation so no Sigma; web telemetry only, hence Defender/FDR/AWS empty. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/flowise-unauthenticated-oauth-secrets-disclosure-via-api-v1-loginmethod-endpoint
ATT&CKT1528 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scheduled bulk token-refresh maintenance job across all stored credentials
  • Flowise instance with many active chatflows legitimately refreshing tokens near-simultaneously on expiry
  • DR/failover warm-up that re-primes all connected-service tokens
  • Load test against the Flowise API
  • Single automation account driving many credentials as designed
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !has "staging" and CsHost !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the distinct credentialIds successfully refreshed in the bin and the source IP(s); confirm it is not a sanctioned maintenance job. 2) Contain: block source, upgrade to Flowise >=3.1.3, and treat every credentialId in the burst as compromised — revoke/rotate each connected-service client secret and refresh token. 3) Hunt: correlate the burst timestamps with connected-service sign-in logs (SigninLogs, CloudAppEvents, GitHub/Google audit) for token use from the same or attacker-linked IPs; expand the window to catch a slow-and-low variant under threshold.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/"
| where ScStatus == 200
| summarize SuccessfulRefreshes = count(), DistinctCredIds = dcount(CsUriStem), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sources = make_set(CIp, 5) by CsHost, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where SuccessfulRefreshes >= 5 and DistinctCredIds >= 5   // >=5 distinct credentials refreshed in one 5-min bin = token harvest
| order by SuccessfulRefreshes desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as successful_refreshes, dc(Web.url) as distinct_credids, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/*" Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where successful_refreshes >= 5 AND distinct_credids >= 5
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - successful_refreshes
| tstats summariesonly=false count as successful_refreshes, dc(Web.url) as distinct_credids, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/*" Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

High-privilege OAuth consent grant to Flowise application (offline_access / Mail / Files) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces Entra ID consent grants to the Flowise app that include offline_access or read/write mail/file scopes — these are what populate Flowise's stored refresh_tokens that CVE-2026-70478 subsequently leaks. Flags the persistence pre-condition and any newly-widened grant. Rationale: The article states stored credentials contain clientId, clientSecret and refresh_token; offline_access is exactly the scope that yields a refresh_token, and Mail/Files scopes define the blast radius of a stolen token. Scoping the grant to the 'Flowise' app name keeps it article-specific rather than a generic illicit-consent rule. Falcon/CloudWatch empty as this is Entra ID / MCAS telemetry the FDR and AWS trails do not carry; Splunk empty as no equivalent CIM AAD consent dataset is standard here. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/flowise/CVE-2026-70478/ • https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/security/advisories/GHSA-6f7g-v4pp-r667
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1528
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-time setup of a Flowise Google/Microsoft connector by an admin (expected offline_access grant)
  • Re-consent after a scope change during normal Flowise integration expansion
  • Tenant-wide admin consent applied to Flowise as part of sanctioned onboarding
  • A differently-named but legitimate internal app containing 'Flowise' in its display name
  • Bulk consent migration during tenant restructuring
Suppression filter
| where Actor !in ("admin-onboarding@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com")  // add sanctioned onboarding admins after baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm who granted consent (Actor/AccountDisplayName), whether they are an admin, and whether the grant is expected onboarding vs. an unexpected scope widening; note the exact scopes. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke the service principal's OAuth2PermissionGrants and disable the app registration; ensure the underlying Flowise deployment is patched to >=3.1.3 so stored refresh tokens can't be leaked. 3) Hunt: for each granted credential, check the web-access UCs for refresh-endpoint hits and review connected-service audit logs for token use; enumerate all apps holding offline_access + Mail/Files to find similar exposure.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.", "Add delegated permission grant.", "Add app role assignment grant to user.")
| where RawEventData has "Flowise"
| where RawEventData has_any ("offline_access", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Read", "Mail.Send", "Files.ReadWrite", "Files.Read")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName in~ ("Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add app role assignment grant to user")
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources.displayName)
| where AppName has "Flowise"
| mv-expand mp = TargetResources.modifiedProperties
| extend PropName = tostring(mp.displayName), NewVal = tostring(mp.newValue)
| where PropName has_any ("ConsentAction.Permissions", "DelegatedPermissionGrant.Scope", "AppRole.Value")
| where NewVal has_any ("offline_access", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Read", "Mail.Send", "Files.ReadWrite", "Files.Read")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, AppName, PropName, NewVal
| order by TimeGenerated desc
